body:
I think it should be possible to optimize `is_readable_from_caller_thread` (which is used from `ERR_READ_THREAD_GUARD_V`). 

We're currently using `thread_local` 2x, which is quite slow.
Since only one thread is safe for accessing `Node` (or all are at once), it should be possible to store the safe thread ID instead (atomic if need be; would still be a bit slow but faster than `thread_local`). 
I tried this (https://github.com/Ivorforce/godot/tree/thread-check-fast), but unfortunately it isn't _this_ easy - I'm guessing some thread isn't "re-activating" their access to `Node` after another thread gets access, which is something that makes sense in the current implementation, but wouldn't be possible in the new one. So it would need some additional reformatting to make it work.

In your benchmark however it looks like `ERR_READ_THREAD _GUARD_V(false);` is taking just as much time (even less) than accessing the `data.visible` variable. This doesn't really make sense to me, but I don't know how your profiler works.

> In your benchmark however it looks like ERR_READ_THREAD _GUARD_V(false); is taking just as much time (even less) than accessing the data.visible variable. This doesn't really make sense to me, but I don't know how your profiler works.

Generally when looking at c++ source code and timings you have to use a bit of interpretation in my experience. What the c++ translates to in assembly can be rather more complex in some cases, so sometimes looking at the assembly timings can help. Also cache misses can occur higher up than you would think, costs can be moved around considerably, particularly on entering and leaving function.

I'll double check this my end too, I have to go out now will be back later this afternoon.

UPDATE: Have checked this by profiling again, same results.

> In your benchmark however it looks like ERR_READ_THREAD _GUARD_V(false); is taking just as much time (even less) than accessing the data.visible variable. This doesn't really make sense to me, but I don't know how your profiler works.

I'm not sure I understand? Returning `data.visible` is a simple operation, whereas the thread guard probably has a branch.
Also as said, we are prevent inlining, which adds calling / return costs (which probably dwarf getting the variable, unless it is not in cache).

The actual instructions for reading `data.visible` are only:
```
movzbl 0x480(%rbx),%ebx
and    $0x40,%bl
shr    $0x6,%bl
mov    %ebx,%eax
```
In plain english:

> The instructions extract the 7th bit (bit 6) from a byte located at memory address %rbx + 0x480, place it in the least significant bit of %bl, and then copy the resulting 32-bit value (with only the lowest bit potentially set) into %eax. Essentially, it checks if the 7th bit of that byte is 1 or 0 and stores that result in %eax.

(This is because we are storing `data.visible` in a bitfield, but these costs are pretty low as it is branchless and CPUs are good at this kind of thing. Essentially it just reads the data, performs an AND, then can do anything appropriate, it might not need to SHR or move into EAX depending what the surrounding instructions need to do. That is just to meet the contract of the non-inlined function.)
